newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Focus on Greenspan, data, supply.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK-Focus on Greenspan, data, supply.

text.p: The upcoming week may be short in length for the U.S. Treasury market, but is long in terms of market-moving news which have the potential to push bond yields to new highs or recent lows, players said.

The market is closed Monday in observance of Martin Luther King Jr day, but the following four days promise to be action-packed as the market has to digest fresh Treasury supply, key economic data and more comments from Federal Reserve officials.
When the dust settles at the end of next week, market participants forsee the 30-year bond yield as low as 6.70 percent or up near 7 percent.
The 30-year bond late in the Friday trading session was at 6.83 percent. Players noted that the market has improved since falling sharply after last Friday's employment report.

"I am impressed the way the market has handled bad news, like the employment report and (hawkish) comments from Fed officials, and neutral news such as Tuesday's retail sales and consumer price data," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.
"The message is that money needs to be put to work," he said. "There is a lot of cash on the sidelines."
Whether investors will want to put money to work in the upcoming week depends on the way the market behaves during the four days the market trades.
Players will barely have time to savor their long holiday weekend, when on Tuesday morning the market is welcomed back by Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to the Senate banking committee.
"Greenspan almost certainly will have significant market impact," Dimick said.

"If he says something about stock market exuberance or wage inflation pressures, the market will sell off sharply," he said. "But if he chooses to say nothing and stick to a bland picture of moderate economic growth and moderate inflation there will be a relief trade higher."
John McAuley, economist at Zions First National Bank, said he expects Greenspan to take the hawkish route, following in the line of other Fed officials' comments the past week.
"They are all preparing the market a little that the majority are thinking there could be tighter policy," McAuley said.
He said with the strong tone of recent data the past month and with fourth quarter growth around 4 percent, the Fed realizes growth is well above its trend potential.

The Commerce Department on Wednesday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT will release December housing starts data. Economists forecast about a 3 percent drop in starts, which should be supportive of Treasury prices, players said.
But at 1200 EST/1700 GMT, the Fed's Beige Book is due, which could pose problems for the market should it point to continued wage pressures.

Also Wednesday, the Treasury will sell $17.5 billion two-year notes, which will be followed by the sale of $12.5 billion five-year notes Thursday. Players do not expect the auctions to go particularly well.

"At 6 percent, two-year notes don't offer enough compensation for a threat of Fed tightening in the first quarter," Dimick said, adding that five-year notes at 6.30 percent are also unattractive. "We need the issues 15 basis points cheaper by auction time."
Players also said other problems facing the market include much more supply and the all important employment cost index report in the next few weeks.
Meanwhile the market will keep an eye on the dollar and corporate supply, said traders.
The heavy corporate supply the past week weighed on Treasuries and players wonder if that will continue next week as the market has more items in its own backyard to worry about it.
Also, the dollar's rise to record levels against the yem, Swiss Franc and mark is seen keeping an underlying tone in the market by encouraging foreign buyers.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
